messages.content: Write a recap post about what a team learned at an industry conference. Around 250 words.

**Three days at [Conference]. The best thing we heard was in a hallway.**

Five of us went. We came home with stickers, a shared cold, and one thing none of us wanted to say out loud.

We planned the trip around the keynote track. That was the error. The keynotes were smooth, thoroughly rehearsed, and mostly made of material the speakers had already posted on their own blogs back in [month]. The learning happened in the margins: over lunch, in a corridor, in the ten minutes before a session started, when an engineer from [Company] mentioned that their [migration/rollout] had taken fourteen months instead of the six they'd announced from the stage.

That one number moved our roadmap further than any deck did.

Other things stayed with us. [Name] sat in on the [topic] workshop and came back certain we've been fixing [problem] a layer too high; we're prototyping her version this sprint. Two unrelated teams told us they'd dropped [tool/approach] for exactly the reason we've been quietly nervous about, which was oddly comforting. And nobody we asked had a tidy answer for [open question]. Everyone is winging it. So are we.

Next year we do this differently. Fewer bodies in seats, more hours in conversation. We'll pick five companies in advance, ask them for coffee, and show up with specific questions rather than hoping the right session appears on the schedule.

Slides are at [link] if you want them. The good stuff isn't in them.

output:
**Three days at [Conference]. The most useful thing anyone told us happened between sessions.**

Five of us flew out. We brought back stickers, a shared cold, and one conclusion nobody wanted to be first to say.

We built the trip around the keynote track. Wrong call. The keynotes were polished and heavily rehearsed, and a good half of the content had already gone up on the speakers' own blogs back in [month]. What we actually learned came from the edges of the schedule: a lunch table, a corridor, the ten idle minutes before a talk, where an engineer from [Company] mentioned their [migration/rollout] had run fourteen months rather than the six they'd promised from the stage.

That single figure changed our roadmap more than any slide deck did.

A few other things stuck. [Name] sat through the [topic] workshop and came home convinced we've been patching [problem] one layer too high. We're prototyping her version this sprint. Two teams with nothing to do with each other told us they'd abandoned [tool/approach], both for the reason we've been privately nervous about, which felt strangely reassuring. And not one person we asked had a clean answer for [open question]. Everybody is improvising. So are we.

We'll run it differently next year. Fewer seats filled, more hours talking. Pick five companies ahead of time, ask each of them for coffee, and turn up with real questions instead of trusting the schedule to produce them.

Slides are at [link] if you want them. The useful part isn't in them.
